title: The sand mandala
hookLine: monks build a palace of colored sand grain by grain, and then sweep it into a jar

cards: A low square table in a museum lobby. Around it, a few Tibetan monks lean in so close their noses nearly touch the surface.
Each holds a thin metal funnel and rubs a rod along its ridged side, and the vibration lets out colored sand, a few grains at a time. A thin blue line. A red petal.

A gold edge. Visitors come back day after day to watch the circle grow, more detailed than seems possible. Then, at the end, the monks chant, pick up brushes, and sweep the whole thing from the edges into the center.

teach.b: Mandala is a Sanskrit word for a circle. In Tibetan Buddhism a mandala is a picture of an awakened world, often drawn as a palace seen from above, with a buddha or deity at the center and gates opening in each direction.
First, it's a map, not a decoration. Every color, symbol and line has a meaning in the practice it belongs to.
A sand mandala is usually made for a particular ceremony, and those who use it in practice learn to visualize the palace in their minds.
Second, the making is itself practice. The monks work with chanting and concentration, grain by grain. A shaky hand or a sneeze can undo an hour.
Patience isn't a side effect; it's part of the offering. Third, the sweep. When the ceremony is done, the mandala is dismantled on purpose, with prayers.
Some of the sand is given to people watching as a blessing, and the rest is often carried to a river or other flowing water and poured in, so the blessing travels on. Fourth, why sweep it at all?

Buddhist teaching holds that everything made of parts comes apart: impermanence. The sweep makes that teaching visible. All that skill, all that beauty, and the hand that made it is the hand that clears it away.
For some watching, the sweep doesn't look like a loss. It looks like the last step of the work.

how: Tibetan monks make sand mandalas for particular ceremonies, working with chanting and fine metal funnels, and when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala with prayers, sharing some sand and pouring the rest into flowing water.

o: glue it down and keep it.
give the whole thing to a museum.
games.why: it's swept away, edges to center, with prayers, to make impermanence visible. the sweeping is the last step of the work.

practice: Gather a few small things within reach, coins, pens, keys, a leaf, a cup, and slowly arrange them into a small pattern with a center, taking care with each one.
Then, with the same care, gather it all back up, one piece at a time, and put each thing where it came from. Notice what the letting go feels like in your hands.

wordCard.voice: The sand mandala. A Tibetan picture of an awakened world, built grain by grain for a ceremony, and then swept away to show that everything made comes apart. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sweep it away. Even something beautiful is allowed to end. That's today, done.
